title: Sujeet Kalkal's Comeback From 2-9 Down Wins Asian Games Wrestling Gold
excerpt: The 23-year-old Indian beat Tajikistan's Abdulmazhid Kudiev 10-9 in the men's 65kg freestyle final at Aichi-Nagoya on October 2, ending India's eight-year wait for an Asian Games wrestling gold.
body:
• Sujeet Kalkal, 23, won the men's 65kg freestyle wrestling gold at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games 2026, defeating Tajikistan's Abdulmazhid Kudiev 10-9 in the final on October 2.
  • Trailing 2-9 with about 100 seconds remaining, Kalkal scored eight unanswered points — four takedowns — and sealed the win with a final takedown with just 11 seconds left on the clock.
  • The semifinal was no easier: he beat reigning Olympic champion Kotaro Kiyooka of Japan to reach the gold-medal bout, after throwing Iran's Abbas Ebrahimzadehsavadkouhi from a standing position within 20 seconds of their quarterfinal.
  • The gold ended India's eight-year wait for an Asian Games wrestling title, going back to Bajrang Punia and Vinesh Phogat in Jakarta 2018, and continued India's 65kg lineage after Yogeshwar Dutt (2014) and Bajrang Punia (2018).

Sujeet Kalkal was seven points down with a minute and 40 seconds left in his Asian Games final. Eleven seconds from the end, he was an Asian champion. The 23-year-old Indian wrestler completed one of the most dramatic comebacks in Asian Games wrestling history on October 2, fighting back from 2-9 down to beat Tajikistan's Abdulmazhid Kudiev 10-9 and win the men's 65kg freestyle gold at Aichi-Nagoya 2026.

The comeback, point by point

Kudiev had dominated the opening period, scoring nine points while restricting Kalkal to two. The second period began with the Indian needing a dramatic change — and he found it almost immediately. About 1:20 into the period, Kalkal secured a takedown to cut the deficit to 4-9, then attacked again before Kudiev could reset: 6-9. With just over a minute remaining, another two-point takedown made it 8-9.

https://x.com/MIB_India/status/2107362772564705703

Kudiev, who had dictated the opening period, was suddenly defending, trying to run down the clock. Kalkal kept attacking the legs, and with 11 seconds left he completed one final takedown. The scoreboard moved to 10-9 — eight unanswered points in the second period — and the final whistle confirmed the result.

The road through the draw

The final was not the first time Kalkal had stared down a favorite. After a comfortable opening victory, he threw Iran's Abbas Ebrahimzadehsavadkouhi from a standing position within the opening 20 seconds of their quarterfinal. The semifinal brought an even bigger test: Olympic champion Kotaro Kiyooka of Japan. Kalkal beat him too, reaching the gold-medal bout with a simple plan — wrestle his own way, trust his preparation and strength, and fight for every single point.

"This gold means a lot to me. Not just because it is an Asian Games gold, but because there is so much behind this medal."

— Sujeet Kalkal, speaking to TimesofIndia.com

Two years after Dubai

In 2024, Kalkal was stranded at Dubai International Airport for three days after floods disrupted his travel to Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, for the Asian Olympic Qualifying Tournament. By the time a flight was arranged, it was too late — and with it went his chance to qualify for the Paris Olympics. The disappointment, he says, is now behind him. What remains is the lesson, and a much bigger target.

Los Angeles 2028 is, in his words, obviously a very big goal — and he wants to get there on his own terms: not merely to participate, but to win gold.

"Fear may never completely go away, but now I know how to fight with fear."

— Sujeet Kalkal

Ending an eight-year wait

India had not won a wrestling gold at the Asian Games since Bajrang Punia and Vinesh Phogat stood atop the podium in Jakarta in 2018. Kalkal's win slots him into India's proud 65kg lineage — Yogeshwar Dutt won the weight class in 2014, Bajrang Punia in 2018. The Indian Olympic Association has named Kalkal the first recipient of its new Raja Randhir Singh Award, instituted to honor the best male sportsperson of the Asian Games.

He dedicated the gold to the whole of India, and his first call went to his father, Dayanand, in Imlota village in Bhiwani, Haryana — the family that supported the football-playing boy who became an Asian champion. He later told NDTV that winning gold for India felt like Diwali to him.

What's next

Kalkal, the world No. 2 in the 65kg category, leaves Aichi-Nagoya with the biggest title of a career that already includes an U23 World Championship crown, Asian Championships success and a Zagreb Open triumph. India's wrestling campaign finished with six medals — golds for Kalkal and Aman (57kg), silvers for Antim Panghal and Nitesh Siwach, bronzes for Deepak Punia and Sunil Kumar — its best Asian Games showing in more than six decades. The next target is Los Angeles. "Gold ke liye jaana hai," Kalkal said — if you're going to the Olympics, go to win gold.
image_caption: Sujeet Kalkal celebrates with the Indian tricolor after his Asian Games victory. The 23-year-old fought back from 2-9 down to beat Tajikistan's Abdulmazhid Kudiev 10-9 in the men's 65kg freestyle final at Aichi-Nagoya on October 2.
nri_angle: A 23-year-old from Bhiwani's stunning comeback ended an eight-year gold drought — the kind of underdog sporting moment that rallies the global Indian diaspora around the tricolor.
